prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It's true: I have it though I hardly approve of anything it does. Supposed bend of light or smudge where two odd angles cross. I hardly see— can hardly do a thing with it. White zone of no flesh pressing into no. So low, I can’t scale or measure it. I used to think: OK! A clean sharp place to keep. Or: I'll growa thing! to keep, for me! But no. It's just a ward to mark & mount, a loop I lope around with, so I count myself a realm of realms. I vote & vote. Turns out, we agree with everything we do, almost. We sweep the precincts of ourselves: the rooms between each rib & under them till we reach the fat red condo where our blood leans in. We live here now. Half heart, half townhouse. Come on down. Turn on that sweet TV. Our mise en place, our rugs & nooks: we’re full of stuff. We paint the furniture we couldn’t live without. It’s true at last: we have it all though we hardly know what any of it does.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker possesses something (perhaps a body, self, or space) they can barely understand, measure, or approve of, describing it as a strange, hard-to-grasp "white zone."
- Initial hopes of finding a clean, useful, or generative space have given up to disappointment, revealing instead just a boundary or marker to circle around.
- The self is portrayed as a self-contained "realm of realms," where the speaker constantly agrees with and votes for their own actions almost by default.
- The body is metaphorically mapped as a domestic space—ribs as rooms, blood as a "condo"—suggesting we inhabit our own physical existence like a home filled with comforts and belongings.
- The piece concludes that we accumulate and surround ourselves with things (both literal and existential) despite still not truly understanding their purpose or function.

Keywords: Supposed, White, But

outputs.L1:
This piece reads like an intentionally fragmented, image-driven prose poem—the broken syntax ("I hardly see—can hardly do a thing with it"), unconventional wordplay ("growa thing"), and abrupt tonal shifts ("Come on down. Turn on that sweet TV.") seem to be deliberate stylistic choices rather than errors needing correction.

Before I proceed, I want to flag a tension: standard "polishing" for eloquence and professionalism would typically mean:
- Smoothing fragmented syntax into complete sentences
- Removing colloquialisms ("Come on down")
- Standardizing unusual constructions
- Creating more conventional transitions

But these are likely the very features giving the piece its poetic voice and emotional texture (the disorientation, the intimacy, the strange humor). If I "polish" it in the conventional sense, I risk erasing what makes it distinctive—turning a poem into generic prose.

Could you clarify your goals for this revision? For example:
1. **Preserve the poetic/experimental register**, but tighten word choice, rhythm, and imagery for more precision and resonance (a poetry-editing approach)
2. **Convert it into standard professional prose**, sacrificing the fragmented style for clarity and conventional grammar (essentially rewriting the genre)
3. **Something in between**—smoothing rough patches while keeping the surreal, poetic quality intact

Knowing which direction you want will help me actually serve the text rather than flatten it into something it isn't trying to be.

Here's a rewrite that preserves the facts while using different language and structure:

It's real: this thing belongs to me, even though I barely endorse whatever it accomplishes. Maybe it's light warping, or perhaps just a blur forming where two strange angles intersect. I struggle to perceive it—can barely operate it at all. A pale territory of absent flesh, pushing against emptiness. It sits so low that no measurement can capture it. Once, I imagined: Perfect! A pristine, defined space to hold onto. Or perhaps: I'll cultivate something here—something that's mine to keep! But that wasn't right either. It's merely a boundary marker, a circuit I circle endlessly, which lets me claim myself as a territory made of territories. I cast ballots repeatedly. As it turns out, we're in agreement with nearly everything we undertake. We inspect the districts of our own being: the spaces between and beneath each rib, until we arrive at that dense crimson chamber where our blood settles in. This is where we reside now. Part cardiac muscle, part row house. Stop by anytime. Switch on that beloved television. Our workspace setup, our carpets and corners: we're brimming with possessions. We decorate the furnishings we simply cannot part with. And finally it's confirmed: everything belongs to us, though we scarcely understand what any of it does.
outputs.L3:
# The White Zone

There is a territory I claim as mine, though I can barely chart its borders or take its measure. I possess it the way one possesses a fog—aware of its presence, unable to grasp its shape. Perhaps it is my body. Perhaps it is something closer to a self, or further, a kind of internal space I've been given no proper instrument to survey. I call it, for lack of better language, a white zone: blank not from emptiness but from an excess of ambiguity, a strangeness that resists my attempts at understanding, resists even my attempts at approval.

I had hoped for more from this territory. I imagined, at some point, that I might find within it something clean—a workspace, perhaps, or a wellspring, some generative clearing where things could be built or grown. I pictured usefulness. I pictured purpose humming quietly beneath the surface, waiting to be tapped. But that hope has thinned into disappointment, and what remains is far less than I imagined: not a clearing but a boundary, not a wellspring but a marker in the ground. I am left circling it, the way one circles a stone whose meaning has been lost to time—present, undeniable, but silent.

And yet within this uncertain territory, I remain sovereign. The self is a realm of realms, a nation built entirely of its own citizenry, where every impulse is both proposal and parliament. I vote for my own actions almost without noticing the ballot has been cast. Agreement arrives before deliberation; consent is less a decision than a reflex. I am ruler and ruled, and the vote is nearly always unanimous, because there is no one else in the chamber to dissent.

If this territory is a nation, then the body is its architecture—rooms built of bone, hallways of nerve and muscle. The ribs curve like the beams of a house, holding the shape of something meant to be inhabited. The blood moves through it all like a tenant who has signed a long lease, circulating through the halls of the self as though this were simply home, a condo furnished with the ordinary comforts of pulse and breath. We do not build ourselves so much as move into ourselves, arranging what we're given as best we can.

And so we gather things—objects, memories, habits, beliefs—filling the rooms of this strange residence with furniture whose purpose we can't always name. We surround ourselves with what we hope will make the space feel more like a home, more like something understood. But still the white zone persists at the center of it all, patient and unexplained, and still we live inside it, decorating the unknown with everything we can find, hoping that accumulation might, eventually, resemble comprehension.
outputs.L4:
**Interior, with No Instruments to Measure It**

I keep calling it *the bend of light*
because I don't know what else to call
the place where I turn away from myself
and find myself still there, waiting,
arms crossed like a question.

Some days it's a white zone—
blank as a room before the movers come,
before anyone decides where the couch goes,
before anyone decides anything at all.
Some days it's a ward,
sterile and hushed, the kind of quiet
that means something is being monitored,
though no one will tell you what.

I have tried to furnish this space.
I have brought in chairs, brought in light fixtures,
brought in the blood that moves through me
without asking permission, the ribs
that curve like the beams of a house
I did not build but somehow inherited.
A townhouse of bone. A narrow hallway
of breath. I walk through myself
and touch the walls to make sure
they're still standing.

We vote & vote—
on what to keep, what to let go of,
on whether the past deserves a seat
at this table we never agreed to set.
We're full of stuff: opinions, organs,
old arguments we lost and carried home
anyway, wrapped in tissue paper,
placed on a shelf we dust
out of habit, not affection.

I thought if I gathered enough—
enough memory, enough matter,
enough rooms inside the one room—
I would finally understand
what it is I am guarding.
But possession is not comprehension.
You can own a house and never know
which pipe feeds which faucet,
which wall is load-bearing,
which window was always painted shut.

I have it all now, whatever *all* means—
the light bent at its familiar angle,
the white zone humming its low static,
the ward with its single flickering bulb.
I have the ribs, the blood, the furniture,
the endless small elections of the self,
deciding and deciding
until deciding becomes its own kind of noise.

And still, when I ask *what is this*,
the room says nothing.
The blood says nothing.
The vote comes back split, inconclusive,
and I am left here again,
surrounded by everything I own,
understanding none of it,
calling it *it*
because *it* is the only word
that fits in the space
where an answer should be.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of Assumptions

Supposed to be simple, that's what they told her. Just fill out the forms, wait for approval, move forward with life as planned.

The walls were white—sterile, institutional white that seemed to absorb sound and hope in equal measure. She sat in that waiting room for three hours, watching the clock's second hand crawl across its face, wondering if patience was a virtue or just another word for powerlessness.

But nothing about bureaucracy moves the way it's supposed to.

Her application had been perfect. Every document signed, every box checked, every deadline met with time to spare. She had done everything right, followed every rule laid out before her, trusted the system to work as it claimed it would.

But trust, she was learning, is not the same as guarantee.

The woman behind the desk—kind eyes, tired smile—finally called her name. The words that followed weren't the ones she'd prepared for. Not rejection exactly, but something worse: indefinite delay. More forms. More waiting. More white walls to stare at while her life remained suspended between what was supposed to happen and what actually would.

She walked out into the afternoon light, blinking against the sudden brightness after so many hours in that colorless room. The world outside hadn't paused for her small crisis. Traffic moved. People walked with purpose toward destinations she couldn't imagine.

Supposed to be simple. But simple, she was discovering, was a luxury reserved for someone else's story.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about the body as a house, blending anatomy with domestic imagery like furniture, TV, and rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
# The House of Bone and Breath

Enter through the mouth, that ever-open door, and mind the threshold of teeth—white pickets guarding a garden of tongue. The hallway of throat leads down, down, past the coat closet of collarbone where old winters hang forgotten.

The heart lives in the parlor, always. It sits in its favorite chair, rocking rocking rocking, a metronome nobody wound but nobody can stop. Sometimes it hosts guests—grief comes for tea, joy stays too long at parties, and love rearranges the furniture without asking, leaves fingerprints on every surface.

Down the spine's staircase—mind the vertebrae, they creak like floorboards remembering older houses, houses that stood before this one, houses that fell.

In the belly-kitchen, something is always cooking, some slow stew of hunger and memory, and the pilot light of intuition flickers blue and constant beneath the ribs' cabinets, beneath the good dishes nobody uses.

The lungs are the television, endlessly playing static and symphony, tuning in to the weather of the world—storms in the news, sunshine through the gauze curtains of alveoli. Turn up the volume when the silence gets too loud. Breathe. That's the remote control. That's the only channel.

Upstairs, the mind's attic: boxes of yesterday stacked to the rafters, photographs developing in the dark, a rocking horse of old fears nobody's ridden in years but everybody still dusts.

The eyes are windows, obviously—but whose house are we in, exactly, when the windows look both ways? When the neighbors (other bodies, other houses) peer back through their own reflective glass, and everyone waves, and everyone wonders who is watching whom sleep?

Hands are the porch lights, always signaling *someone is home, someone is home*, even when the house feels emptiest, even when the mail piles up unread in the mouth's mailbox, tongue-shaped, waiting for words that don't arrive.

At night, the whole house settles—hinges of hip, sockets of shoulder—into the dark hum of its own breathing walls. The furnace of the heart keeps burning low. Somewhere, a door left ajar. Somewhere, the television murmurs itself to sleep. And you, small ghost, wander room to room in your own architecture, turning off lights, checking locks, forever moving in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a strange, first-person poem that starts with "It's true: I have it though I hardly approve of anything it does," exploring self-ownership and confusion about one's own body.
counterfactuals.output:
# Custody

It's true: I have it though I hardly approve of anything it does—
this body that sweats when I am calm,
that craves salt at 3 a.m. like it's paying off a debt
I never signed for. I file complaints
into the small office of my skull.
No one answers. No one is hiring.

I am the landlord of a house
that keeps rearranging its own furniture,
moving the heart closer to the exit,
letting the lungs forget their one job
mid-sentence, mid-kiss, mid-anything.
I wake up and check the locks
though I never remember installing doors.

Sometimes it grows hair where I did not ask,
softens in places I demanded firmness,
aches in a joint I don't recall purchasing.
I want to return it. I want the receipt.
Instead I get this: a knee that predicts rain,
a scar that outlived the reason for it,
a mouth that says the wrong name
in the dark like it's testing me.

I have owned this thing for decades
and still don't know where the manual went,
if there ever was one, if the previous owner
left it in worse shape than they found it
or if I did that part myself,
slowly, the way you ruin
something you love by loving it too specifically.

People say *listen to your body*
like it speaks a language I signed up for.
It says nothing. It grumbles. It performs
small betrayals in supermarkets, in elevators,
in rooms where I am trying to be
someone slightly more impressive than this.

And yet—when it sleeps, I sleep.
When it grieves, I find out through the throat,
the way water finds out through a crack
that it was always going somewhere lower.
I did not choose this vessel.
I only found myself already in it,
already moving, already
being carried by the very thing
I keep insisting I am steering.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental piece of poetic prose that treats the heart as real estate—half heart, half townhouse—using playful, disjointed syntax.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Sale By Owner: One (1) Ventricle, Slightly Used

Open concept. That's what they'll say, the listing agents of the interior, when they walk you through — *this way to the atrium, mind the step, the previous tenant left in a hurry, didn't patch the walls where the pictures hung.*

Charming fixer-upper. Original details throughout. Exposed brick where someone's fist went through in '09, never repaired, we call it *character* now, we call it *authentic*.

Two bedrooms if you count the one that's actually a hallway pretending. Actually a threshold. Actually the place between rooms where you stand deciding whether to enter or leave, and mostly you just stand there, mostly you just stand.

*Cozy* — meaning small. Meaning: this heart, this house, was never built for two, was built for one who then invited someone in anyway, foolish, the way houses always are foolish about who they let cross the threshold. Come in. Take off your shoes. Take off whatever else you're carrying.

Foundation: solid, mostly, structurally sound except for the crack that runs from basement to attic, that runs from first love to last, you can feel the draft in December, you can feel it any month really, the wind gets in no matter how many times you say *there is no wind, there is no crack, this house is fine.*

Recently renovated — meaning: someone left, and someone stayed, and the staying-one painted over everything, tried anyway, the paint didn't take, the walls kept bleeding through their old color like a bruise that won't.

Nearby amenities: grief (walking distance), joy (further, you'll need a car), the old grocery where you bought flowers for someone who's now just a name you don't say. Good school district for whatever you're trying to teach yourself twice now, the same lesson, the same *don't, don't, you already know how this—*

Won't last long at this price. Won't last long at any price. Everything sells eventually, even this, even the rooms nobody wanted, even the attic where you keep what you can't look at directly, even the heart, especially the heart, up for grabs, up for grabs, *please,* someone, make an offer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that mixes political language ("vote," "precincts") with bodily and domestic imagery to explore themes of self-governance and identity.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Body Politic

I am my own precinct now,
a district of one, gerrymandered
by scars into strange shapes—
here the redistricting of grief,
there the ward where hope
still holds its slim majority.

Each morning I canvass myself,
knock on the door of my ribs,
ask the tired heart if it will vote
again for waking, for the long
campaign of getting dressed,
of turning toward the window's
small democracy of light.

The kitchen is a polling place.
I stand in line behind my own
hesitations, cast my ballot
for the coffee over the wine,
for the phone call I keep
tabling like a bill no one
will sponsor. Motion to adjourn
denied. The session of the self
runs late again.

In the bathroom mirror,
a town hall meeting—
every insecurity gets its turn
at the microphone, filibusters
in the language of *not enough*,
while I, the moderator, learn
to bang the gavel, to say
*your time has expired.*

Sovereignty is this:
the right to seal my own envelope,
to trust the count of my own hands
when they cup water, or a face,
or nothing at all, just air,
practicing the shape of yes.

I elect, some days, to stay in bed—
a filibuster of my own devising,
a recess called by executive order
of the exhausted nervous system.
Other days I ratify the morning
like an amendment long overdue,
sign my name to sunlight,
to the long slow work
of self-rule.

No one else can enter this booth.
No one else can read
the fine print of my wanting.
I fold the ballot of myself
each night, slide it into the box
of sleep, trust the count
will come back close enough
to true—

this democracy of one,
still counting, still contested,
still, somehow,
mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a whimsical, abstract poem about possessing something intangible (like a soul or consciousness) that you can't fully understand or control, ending with the same line it began with.
counterfactuals.output:
**Tenant**

I keep a small weather system where my heart should be.

It rains on Tuesdays for no reason,
snows in the attic of my left lung,
and once, in April, grew a rainbow
that answered to a different name than mine.

I did not order this. I did not
sign for the delivery of thunder,
yet here it is, pacing my ribs
like a tiger in a room built for a moth.

Some mornings I catch it
trying on my face in the mirror,
practicing my laugh,
getting the corners wrong.

I ask it what it wants.
It answers in barometric pressure,
in the language of gulls
wheeling over a shore I've never seen.

I have tried to cage it in routines,
in meditation apps, in the small
zoo of my daily habits—
it slips out anyway, smelling of ozone.

Perhaps it is not mine to keep.
Perhaps I am the weather
and it is merely
wearing my skin as a coat too big.

Still, we share this address,
this creaking house of bone,
this leaking roof called consciousness—
two strangers arguing over the thermostat
of what it means to be a self.

I keep a small weather system where my heart should be.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
